prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling atomic clocks of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I opened with B012 first and B056 second, and after reading the ballots I now put the optical lattice clock first. The discovery is clear and singular: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the Stark shift while allowing very many atoms to be interrogated at once, and this took fractional uncertainty to the 10^-18 level. It has already enabled tests of fundamental constants and relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, and it underpins the coming redefinition of the second. Independent clocks in several laboratories agree, so the result is mature and not a matter of a single group's claim. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed the concept and realised the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye developed it to the leading accuracy and stability. Opening support is also the broadest, with three first places and six top-three rankings across seven members. This is a discovery-first prize whose people are easy to identify, which is how the committee should reason.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize may look incremental after the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control recognitions, and that it risks reading as another precision-measurement award. There is also a real credit question about contributors outside the two names, such as ion-clock pioneers and other lattice-clock groups (Ludlow, Lemonde and others), and about collective effects work in Ye's group. A further concern is that a two-person AMO prize leaves out the younger, faster-moving fields that the committee might want to recognise while the discoverers are active, and the redefinition of the second has not yet formally happened.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because the magic-wavelength idea gives both high stability and very low systematic uncertainty, with Katori the concept's originator and Ye the driver of record precision, and he judges the overlap with the 2005 prize as distinct.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and I now share the first place. I would qualify the overlap point: Kroll is right that the physics is distinct, but the citation should name the lattice-clock architecture explicitly and not speak generally of precision spectroscopy, otherwise the 2005 and 2012 recognitions make it look like a repeat. Where I differ slightly is that the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the prize-worthy work and not a reason to give it, so I would keep it out of the citation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new organising principle for electronic matter, with the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall state from Kane and Mele and the HgTe realisation by Molenkamp, and treats the 2016 overlap as a committee judgement.
responses.response: I ranked B007 only fourth and still do, and the reason is attribution, which the other members' ballots also raise. The HgTe experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and three-dimensional topological insulators by Moore, Balents, Fu and Hasan sit outside the credited names, so a three-person prize would be contested however important the idea. I accept that the concept is more fundamental than a clock and that it may be the most important of the field-defining candidates. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize, I would sooner give it to the twistronics case, where theory and experiment pair cleanly. I disagree that the 2016 overlap is merely procedural: Kane-Mele is an extension of that conceptual line, which makes the case somewhat less original than it would otherwise be.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube first as the opening of a new observational window for neutrinos, with Halzen as scientific driving force and Karle central to construction and the discovery analysis, and he places the lattice clock third.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously, since neutrino astronomy is the sort of result I think the committee should reward, and I ranked it fifth in my own opening. My difficulty is the same as for any collaboration discovery: the credit rests on the founding vision, the construction and the discovery analysis, and the work of hundreds of people and predecessors such as AMANDA and DUMAND is not captured by two names. That is a heavier attribution burden than the lattice clock carries. I would keep IceCube for a later year when the source identification is firmer rather than put it ahead of the clock now.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators first and the lattice clock third, noting that the credit list leaves out contributors such as Ludlow and Lemonde and that Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is not in the topological-insulator names.
responses.response: The Ludlow and Lemonde point is fair and I flag it among my uncertainties, but the lattice-clock prize needs only the two people who originated the architecture and drove it to record performance, and those who built later implementations are the normal long tail of any prize. This differs from B007, where the omitted theorists were arguably indispensable to the experiment that is credited. That asymmetry is why I treat the two candidates differently despite similar scientific stature.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would see the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether ion-clock and other lattice-clock contributors should be credited, and what weight Ye's collective-effects and laser-coherence work carries relative to Katori's concept.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene is too young given that the superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved, and how the early independent experimental groups should be weighed.
Whether a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize can be made fair without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and how much the 2016 prize reduces its priority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections (PhD supervisor David Gross, mentor Hector Rubinstein, co-author Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theoretical-physics group) do not coincide with any shortlisted candidate or credited name.
